summary: Registers the MIME sub-type multipart/voice-message for use with the Voice Profile for Internet Mail. It marks a message as a voice message made of several parts. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 3801.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a special label for an email that holds a voice message, so mail programs know to treat it as a spoken note and not as plain text.

questions: how are vpim voice messages labeled
what goes in a vpim v2 message
subtitle: A MIME label to mark messages as voice mail.

tldr.problem: Voice messaging systems need a standard way to identify voice mail messages when exchanging them over email.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2423 registers the MIME subtype multipart/voice-message to wrap voice message components (audio, images, contact info) into a single identifiable package that email systems recognize.
tldr.outcome: The multipart/voice-message type became the standard container for Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) messages, but was replaced by RFC 3801 as VPIM evolved.

today: RFC 2423 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 3801, which updated the VPIM v2 specification. The multipart/voice-message type is no longer actively used as VPIM has evolved.

sections.title: Why Voice Mail Needs a Label
sections.content:
The Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) brings voice messaging to email systems. A voice message is not plain text or a simple attachment—it is a structured package that may contain multiple parts: the sender's spoken name, the message subject, the voice content itself, and directory information about the sender. Email systems need a way to recognize and handle these packages correctly.

RFC 2423 defines multipart/voice-message, a MIME subtype specifically designed as a container for VPIM voice messages. This label tells email clients and systems that they are dealing with voice mail, so they can process it appropriately.
sections.plainLanguage: A voice message has several pieces: who it is from (their voice), what it is about, and what they are saying. The email label multipart/voice-message wraps all these pieces together so the email system knows what to do with them.

sections.title: The multipart/voice-message Container
sections.content:
The multipart/voice-message subtype is functionally identical to multipart/mixed, defined in RFC 2046. This means systems that do not recognize multipart/voice-message can safely treat it as a regular mixed container without breaking the message. The difference is semantic: the presence of multipart/voice-message signals that the contents represent a voice message.

A multipart/voice-message container must include two required parameters: boundary (which separates the message parts) and version (which indicates conformance to VPIM version 2.0 or earlier). The version parameter allows future versions of VPIM to maintain backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of multipart/voice-message as a labeled box. Inside the box are the voice recording, the sender's name, and other pieces. The label tells a mail program what kind of box it is.

sections.title: What Goes Inside
sections.content:
A VPIM v2 voice message typically contains multiple parts in this order: a spoken name segment (the sender's voice saying their name), a spoken subject segment (the sender's voice stating the topic), and the voice message itself. Additional parts may include images and directory information about the message sender.

The spoken name must not exceed 12 seconds; the spoken subject must not exceed 20 seconds. Only specific media types are allowed inside a v2 container: audio/*, image/*, message/rfc822 and application/directory. This restriction ensures that VPIM systems can reliably process voice messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A voice message typically has three parts: first, the sender says their name (up to 12 seconds), next they state the subject (up to 20 seconds), then comes the message itself. There may also be a picture or contact information.

sections.title: Identifying Voice Messages
sections.content:
RFC 2423 acknowledges a privacy consideration: the multipart/voice-message label explicitly identifies a message as voice mail. In some environments where message content confidentiality is important, this visible labeling could reveal information about message types. However, in most practical email deployments, this is not a significant security concern.

The registration specifies the MIME type's intended usage as COMMON, reflecting broad applicability in voice messaging systems. It includes optional information such as the file extension .VPM and Macintosh file type code VPIM.
sections.plainLanguage: By labeling something as a voice message, anyone looking at the email headers can tell it is voice mail, not a regular email. Usually that is fine, but sometimes it might matter.
